1. Orientation & Logging In

Your admin URL

Everything you do lives in the Shopify admin, not on the public website. Bookmark it:

https://admin.shopify.com/store/arbortechtools

The public storefront is https://arbortechtools.com (and its country variants, see below). Right now the storefront is still password-protected while we finish the build; you'll log in with the store password until launch. That changes nothing about how you use the admin.

Logging in & 2FA

  • Sign in with your personal staff account (never share one login).
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) is required. Use an authenticator app. This protects the store from unauthorised changes.
  • If you get locked out, an owner can reset your access from Settings → Users and permissions.

Quick tour of the sidebar

Sidebar itemWhat lives there
HomeYour dashboard - recent orders, live view, top products, tasks.
OrdersAll customer orders and their statuses (see Section 8).
ProductsProducts, collections, inventory, gift cards. Your most-used area (Section 2).
ContentBlog posts, pages, metaobjects (Settings → Custom data). This is where Pages and Blog live (Section 3).
Online StoreThemes (incl. Customize), Navigation (menus), Pages, Blog posts, URL redirects, domains (Section 4, 5, 7).
AnalyticsStore performance, sales reports, traffic sources.
SettingsPayments, shipping, taxes, users & permissions, notifications, apps. Mostly call-us territory (see Guardrails).
Five markets, one admin

You manage one store with five markets: Australia (/), United States (/en-us), Canada (/en-ca), United Kingdom (/en-uk) and Germany (/de-de, with an English option at /en-de). A product you edit is the same product everywhere; market-specific text (descriptions, story panels) lives in separate fields. When you edit, check whether a field has a market-specific version (see Blind Spots → Metafields).

2. Products & Collections

This is the core of most changes: 116 products today, organised by audience (Woodworking, Masonry/Trade, Landscaping) and by product type.

2.1 Add / edit / duplicate a product

Products → All products lists everything. Click a product to open it, or Add product for a new one.

  • Title - the product name as it appears on the storefront.
  • Description - the main body copy. This theme also pulls a longer, structured description from custom fields (see Blind Spots → Metafields). The main description box is for the short editorial blurb.
  • Media - add images and video (drag and drop). The first image is the collection/thumbnail image.
  • Pricing - price, compare-at price (for "was/now" sales). Prices are set in your market's currency by default; Shopify converts for other markets unless you set market-specific prices.
  • SKU - your internal stock code. This is important: it drives inventory and the packing-slip automation. Keep SKUs matching the master SKU list.
  • Inventory - quantity per location. Shopify tracks stock per warehouse location (AU Perth, US Treeline, CA Barrie, DE, UK).
  • Duplicate - use Duplicate (top right) to copy an existing product as a starting point. Tip: rename it and set status to Draft before editing, so nothing half-finished goes live.

2.2 Product status - active / draft / archived

StatusWhat it means
ActiveVisible and buyable on the storefront.
DraftSaved but hidden. Perfect for preparing a product before launch, or a practice copy.
ArchivedHidden and not for sale, but kept for record. Prefer archive over delete (see Guardrails).
Rule of thumb

Draft first, review, then set to Active. Archive rather than delete. There is no undo for deletions.

2.3 Variants

Some products have options like Voltage (18V / 20V / 54V), Battery platform, Spindle thread, or regional power versions (e.g. 240V UK). Each combination is a variant with its own SKU, price and stock.

  • Add options under the Variants section; Shopify generates the variant grid.
  • Important: this store routes some options per market (e.g. which voltage a country sees). If you add a variant whose option value isn't in the market rules, it may not show in some countries. See Blind Spots → Market option rules.
  • Customers see variant buttons (e.g. 18V / 20V) on the product page.

2.4 Collections - manual vs automated

Products → Collections. A collection is a grouping shown on the shop pages. Your store's collections mirror the old site's shop-online hierarchy:

CollectionHandle (URL)
Woodworking (Power Carving)/collections/power-carving
Woodworking - Power Tools/collections/power-carving-power-tools
Woodworking - Attachments & Accessories/collections/power-carving-attachments-accessories
Masonry / Trade/collections/masonry-trade
Masonry / Trade - Power Tools/collections/masonry-trade-power-tools
Masonry / Trade - Attachments & Accessories/collections/masonry-trade-attachments-accessories
Spare Parts & Consumables/collections/spare-parts-consumables
Power Tools/collections/power-tools
Spare Parts, Blades & Accessories/collections/spare-parts-accessories
Outdoor Grounds Care/collections/outdoor-grounds-care
  • Manual collection - you hand-pick the products. Great for small, curated groups.
  • Automated collection - rules (e.g. tag contains power-tools) pull products in automatically. Most of your shop collections are automated, driven by tags, so tagging a product correctly is how it lands in the right place.

2.5 Product organisation: type, vendor, tags

These three fields drive filtering and navigation across the store:

  • Tags - the most important. Collection rules, the shop filter sidebar (Woodworking / Masonry / Landscaping) and the "By Product" buckets (Power Tools / Attachments & Accessories / Spare Parts & Consumables) all read tags. Key tags: power-tools, attachments-accessories, spare-parts-consumables, woodworking/masonry/landscaping (via power-carving, masonry-trade, outdoor-grounds-care), plus model tags like allsaw, mini-grinder.
  • Product type - e.g. Power Tool / Attachment / Spare Part. Shown on some listing styles.
  • Vendor - Arbortech (or a partner brand like DeWalt where relevant).
Tag carefully

Tagging is how products appear in the right collections and filters. If a product disappears from a shop page after an edit, the tags are the first thing to check. The tag accessories is retired. Use attachments-accessories only.

2.6 Related products: linking accessories to a power tool

The relationship between a power tool and its accessories runs in two directions, and each direction is edited in a different place. Getting this right is how a new blade or attachment shows up everywhere it should.

Direction 1 - the tool page shows its accessories ("Works best with")

Each power tool's product page has an accessories carousel (usually titled "Works best with" or similar). What appears there comes from the power tool's product record:

  1. Open the power tool in Products (not the accessory).
  2. Scroll to the Metafields area at the bottom (click View all if collapsed) and find Related accessories (arbortech.related_accessories).
  3. Click it, then Add product and pick the accessories from the product picker. Drag entries to reorder; the carousel shows them in this order.
  4. Save. The tool's page now lists those accessories with image, price and link.

If that field is empty, the theme falls back through a chain: some products have audience-specific accessory lists (a woodworking visitor and a masonry visitor can be shown different accessories; these override the plain list where they exist), a couple of families (ALLSAW, Power Chisel) have built-in curated lists, and as a last resort Shopify shows automatic recommendations (its own guess, often "customers also bought" products, not necessarily compatible ones).

Rule of thumb

If the accessories shown under a tool look wrong or random, fill in Related accessories on the tool; an explicit list always beats the automatic guess. When you launch a new accessory, add it to every tool it fits.

Direction 2 - the accessory page shows which tools it fits ("Compatible tools")

Each accessory/blade product page has a "Compatible tools" panel linking back to the tools it fits. This is driven by a field on the accessory:

  1. Open the accessory in Products.
  2. In Metafields, find Compatible with (arbortech.compatible_with_filter), a list of tool names, one per entry.
  3. Add the tool name(s) it fits and Save.
Spelling matters - copy, don't retype

These are text labels, matched exactly. The theme uses the same values to link to the tool's page and to build the "Compatible with" filter in the shop sidebar, so AS200X Allsaw and ALLSAW AS200X would count as two different tools and split the filter. Before adding a value, open a similar accessory and copy the exact existing spelling. Generic fitments that aren't Arbortech products (e.g. "Standard Angle Grinder") are fine; they show as an unlinked tile.

Note the compatible-tools panel deliberately does not render on products whose Product type is Power Tool; a tool doesn't list itself. This is another reason the Product type field matters (Section 2.5).

Spare parts - "Associated tool model"

Spare parts and consumables use a third field, Associated tool model (arbortech.associated_tool_model), also a list of tool-name labels on the spare-part product. It powers the tool-model filter shoppers see in the Spare Parts bucket. The same exact-spelling rule applies.

"Configure your order" - add-ons and Bundle with

Power tool pages have a Configure your order area with two groups, each fed by a different field on the tool:

  • Attachments & Accessories add-ons - individual tick-to-add items, driven by the same Related accessories list as "Works best with". Any product can be an add-on; each ticked item is added to the cart as its own line at its normal price, and its own stock is reduced when ordered. If an add-on has a compare-at price higher than its price, its row shows the same struck-through value and orange "Save $X" as a bundle tile, and the order summary lists the saving, so a "discounted when bought with the tool" deal is indicated the same way everywhere.
  • Bundle with tiles - driven by Related bundles (arbt.related_bundles), pointing at bundle products built in Products → Bundles (the Shopify Bundles app). Ticking a tile adds the bundle as one cart line alongside the tool.

Bundle with tiles only appear on products tagged power-tools; accessory pages never show them, by design. If a bundle you assigned isn't showing, check that tag first.

Creating a bundle (and making its discount show)

  1. Products → Bundles → Create bundle. Pick the component products/variants, give the bundle its own title and images. Copy the variant structure (the Market SKU option) from an existing bundle so each country is offered its correct regional version.
  2. Price the discount in, using compare-at. Set the bundle's Price to the discounted amount, and its Compare-at price to the full combined value of the components. This is the native way a bundle discount works; the saving is baked into the bundle product's price. No discount codes are involved.
  3. Assign it to the tool(s): open each power tool → Metafields → Related bundles → add the bundle. The list order is the tile order.
The "Save $X" indicator is automatic

Whenever a bundle's compare-at price is higher than its price, its Bundle-with tile automatically shows the full value struck through next to the discounted price, plus an orange "Save $X". If a bundle tile shows no saving, the compare-at price wasn't set (or isn't higher than the price); that's the whole switch. Set compare-at in each market's pricing too, or overseas shoppers may see no saving (or a converted approximation).

Don't build bundle savings out of discount codes

An automatic "Buy X Get Y" discount (Section 9) also technically discounts items bought together, but it only applies in the cart, so the product page gives shoppers no indication the deal exists. Use bundle pricing (above) for bundle deals; keep Discounts for store-wide or campaign promotions.

Stock behaves itself: a bundle has no inventory of its own; Shopify computes its availability live from the components (tiles grey out as "sold out" automatically), and when an order is placed the bundle line expands so each component's stock is decremented. Nothing to reconcile manually.

2.7 Shop filters - where the sidebar values come from

The filter sidebar on shop pages is built from product data, so a product only appears under a filter if its fields are filled in:

FilterDriven byShown for
Vertical (Woodworking / Masonry / Landscaping)Tags (power-carving, masonry-trade, outdoor-grounds-care)All products
By Product (Power Tools / Attachments & Accessories / Spare Parts & Consumables)Tags (power-tools, attachments-accessories, spare-parts-consumables)All products
Application typeMetafield arbortech.application_typePower tools & accessories
Compatible withMetafield arbortech.compatible_with_filter (same field as 2.6)Accessories bucket
Tool modelMetafield arbortech.associated_tool_modelSpare-parts bucket

The two tag groups and the three metafields do different jobs, and it's worth keeping them straight. Vertical only changes which products are listed - it never changes which filters appear. By Product is the one that decides which of the three contextual filters you get:

You're on a...Filters that appear
Power Tools pageApplication type
Attachments & Accessories pageApplication type + Compatible with
Spare Parts & Consumables pageTool model
Woodworking / Masonry / Landscaping landing pageNone - deliberate, matches the old site
Spare Parts, Blades & AccessoriesNone - different page layout

You pick these three values from a list - you don't type them. If a value you need isn't in the list, ask us to add it rather than working around it. The list is fixed for a good reason: these used to be free-text boxes, and the store ended up holding both Min.FG.600-B and MIN.FG.600-B for the same tool. The sidebar showed two options that looked identical, and each returned only part of the range - a customer after FG.600-B parts found 5 items or 7, never all 12. Fixed August 2026, and the picker now makes it impossible.

A blank field is not neutral - it hides the product. This is the one that catches people out. A product with no Application type still shows in the unfiltered list, then disappears the moment a customer ticks any Application type box. There is no "other" or "unassigned" group for it to fall into. So when you add a product, filling these fields in is not optional polish; leaving one blank removes the product from that filter entirely.

One more thing that looks like a fault but isn't: the same filter shows different options on different pages. A filter only lists values that actually exist among the products on the page you're looking at, with a count beside each. That's why Application type offers four options on Woodworking pages and six on Masonry / Trade - one field, different products in scope.

If a whole filter has vanished rather than a single product, the product fields aren't the cause. Filters also have to be switched on under Apps → Search & Discovery → Filters. Have a look there first, and talk to us before changing anything on that screen - turning one off removes it from every shop page at once.

And if a product is missing from a shop page entirely - not just from a filter - check that it's actually visible on the storefront before hunting through its filter fields. See Blind Spots → Active doesn't always mean visible.

3. Content Pages & Blogs

3.1 Editing an existing page

Online Store → Pages (also under Content → Pages). This is where About, Contact, Support, Sustainability, and the vertical pages (Woodworking, Masonry, Landscaping), Artists & Makers, Project Stories, How-to Guides and Competitions live. The Sitemap tab lists every page on the site, grouped by how editable it is; check there before editing an unfamiliar page.

  • Click a page title to edit. The editor is a rich-text editor with headings, bold/italic, links, lists and images.
  • Save keeps your changes; the page stays live. Preview shows how it looks before you save.
  • Status: Active (visible) or Draft (hidden).
  • Several of your pages are landing pages with bespoke layouts (e.g. the vertical pages, artist pages). For those, the main content area may be secondary to structured blocks; if you need to change the layout, that's a call-us item.

3.2 Creating a new page

  1. Add page → give it a Title (this becomes the URL handle automatically).
  2. Write the body with the rich-text toolbar: Headings for structure, links (select text → link icon), images.
  3. Set a template. For standard pages keep the default; some layouts need a specific template (call us).
  4. Set status: Draft, preview, then publish when happy.
  5. Link it into the site. A published page is invisible until something links to it. Add it to the main or footer menu (Section 4) or link it from another page; otherwise only people with the URL will ever find it.

3.3 Blog posts (the News blog)

Your blog is News (/blogs/news). Online Store → Blog posts → Add blog post:

  • Title → auto-generates the URL.
  • Content - rich-text body.
  • Featured image - the thumbnail shown on the news listing and social shares.
  • Tags - use them for grouping (e.g. product, category, competition).
  • Publishing - set Active now, or schedule a date/time. Scheduled posts show as "Scheduled" until they go live, a "not-yet-live" state to be aware of (see Blind Spots → Draft vs live).
The designed story articles don't use the Content box

The existing story articles (the ones with quote banners, image carousels and video embeds) render from a structured layout field maintained by Juicebox; on those posts, editing the Content box changes nothing on the storefront. Ask us for text, image or layout changes to a story article. New posts you create yourself render the Content box as normal.

5.4 Saving vs publishing theme changes

This store works on a shared dev theme + preview duplicate model:

  • Save in the Customize sidebar writes to the theme you're editing. If that's the published preview theme, changes go live to visitors immediately. If it's an unpublished theme, they're saved but not public.
  • Publish (Theme actions → Publish) makes a theme the live storefront. You should never publish. That's Juicebox's job; we cut a fresh preview duplicate after each code deployment.
  • Practical: when Juicebox deploys new code, a new preview is published. Content edits you made on the old preview are not carried over automatically; keep a note of what you changed so we can re-apply it, or we coordinate the timing.

6. Media & Assets

Settings → Files (or the image picker inside any product/page/section) is where images are stored and reused.

  • Upload once, reuse everywhere. Pick an existing image from Files rather than re-uploading, so you don't create duplicates.
  • Recommended sizes: product images ~1000-1500px on the long side; hero/banner images ~1600-2000px wide; logos 180×180px (favicon). Shopify compresses automatically; start from a good-quality original.
  • File naming: descriptive, lowercase, hyphenated (e.g. allsaw-as200x-gallery-1.jpg). Avoid IMG_0421.jpg; names become part of the image URL and help SEO.
  • Alt text: always fill in the "Alt text" field. It's what screen readers read, what shows when an image fails to load, and it helps search engines understand the image. Describe the image plainly (e.g. "Arbortech AllSaw AS200X cutting a masonry block").

7. SEO Basics

7.1 Page title & meta description

Every product, page, collection and blog post has a "Search engine listing" section (usually bottom-left of the editor, under Search engine listing preview → Edit website SEO).

  • Page title - the title shown in Google results and the browser tab. Keep it descriptive and under ~60 characters.
  • Meta description - the one- or two-sentence summary under the title in search results. Write it like an ad for the page (e.g. "Arbortech AllSaw AS200X - the 54V masonry saw that cuts brick, block and stone. Australian-made, 3-year warranty.").
  • If you leave these blank, Shopify uses the product/page title and content, so filling them in gives you control over how you appear.

7.2 URL handles and changing them

  • The handle is the end of the URL (e.g. /products/allsaw-as200x). It's auto-generated from the title.
  • Changing a handle breaks the old link; anyone with the old URL (including Google) gets a 404. Avoid renaming handles once a page/product is live.
  • If you must change one, create a URL redirect from the old handle to the new one: Online Store → Navigation → URL Redirects → Add redirect (old path → new path). This catches 404s and preserves SEO.

8. Orders & Customers (Awareness Only)

You don't need to manage orders day-to-day, but you should know where they are and what the statuses mean.

  • Orders appear in Orders. Statuses: Open (paid, awaiting fulfilment), Fulfilled (shipped), Unfulfilled, Partially fulfilled, Cancelled, On hold, Draft (not yet placed).
  • Fulfilment is handled by your warehouse team (and the packing-slip automation, see Blind Spots). We won't train order fulfilment in this session; it's deliberately out of scope.
  • Customers are under Customers: every account and every checkout that opts in. You'll find order history and customer details there. This is also where newsletter signups appear as customer records (see Blind Spots).

9. Discounts & Promotions

Discounts (in the sidebar) is fully yours to manage. You set codes, rules and dates; nothing here needs a developer.

  • Discount code - customer types a code at checkout (e.g. CARVE10). Good for campaigns, newsletters, show specials.
  • Automatic discount - applies by itself when the conditions are met (e.g. "10% off all ALLSAW blades"). No code needed; shows in the cart automatically.
  • Types: percentage off, fixed amount off, free shipping, or Buy X Get Y. You can scope any of them to specific products or collections, e.g. a discount on the Woodworking collection only.
  • Set start and end dates when you create it, so promotions switch themselves off; don't rely on remembering to delete them.
  • Combinations - by default discounts don't stack. Each discount has a "Combinations" setting controlling whether it can combine with other product/shipping discounts. Leave stacking off unless you've done the maths.
Discounts apply in every market

A percentage discount applies in all five markets at each market's prices. A fixed-amount discount is set in AUD and converted for other markets; check what "AU$20 off" becomes in USD/GBP/EUR before announcing a round number overseas. "Compare-at" sale pricing (was/now on the product itself) is separate; that's set per product under Pricing (Section 2.1).

10. German Content & Translations

Germany is the one market in a different language. German text lives in several places depending on what kind of text it is:

Kind of textWhere German livesWho edits it
Product titles, descriptions, pages, blog posts, policies, collection descriptionsTranslate & Adapt app (Apps → Translate & Adapt, or the Localize button on a product/page)You - translations are Arbortech's responsibility
Text you type into theme editor sections (homepage modules, footer signup text, copyright, header announcement bar…)Translate & Adapt → German → Themes (step-by-step in 10.1)You - mind the per-theme note in 10.1
Built-in theme labels ("Add to cart", "In stock", form buttons…)Theme locale files, deployed with the theme codeJuicebox - raise a request
Product story panels / Clever BitsSeparate German metaobject lists (the _de variants - see Blind Spots → Metafields)You, via Settings → Custom data
News story articlesSeparate German blog posts (handles starting story-de-), each with its own designed layout (see Section 3.3), not Translate & Adapt. Editing the English story does not touch the German one.Juicebox - raise a request (Section 3.3)
  • In Translate & Adapt, pick German, then the resource type (Products, Pages, Themes, …). Each field shows English on the left, German on the right. Save writes the translation live.
  • Anything left untranslated falls back to English on /de-de. After editing an English description, re-check its German column; the old translation stays until you update it, so the two can drift.
  • AU/US/CA differences (voltage wording, spelling) are not translations; they're market-specific content variants handled through the story-panel market fields, not Translate & Adapt.
  • The German legal pages (Widerruf, Impressum, Datenschutz) are normal pages/policies; keep their German current the same way, and treat them as legally load-bearing. The footer links to them come from the legal menus (see 10.2).

10.1 Translating text you type into theme editor sections

Anything you type into a section in the Theme Editor (homepage modules, footer signup text, copyright text, the header announcement bar…) is translatable per language; no code involved:

  1. Open Apps → Translate & Adapt and pick German.
  2. Choose Themes in the resource list on the left; the same app you already use for products/pages, themes are a resource type in there.
  3. Pick the theme you're working on, then find the section, e.g. Footer. Each field you typed into the Theme Editor shows English on the left, German on the right.
  4. Type the German text and save. It goes live on /de-de immediately; anything left blank shows the English value.
Theme translations are per-theme

Translations you enter are tied to the specific theme you translated. When Juicebox deploys new code and publishes a fresh preview duplicate, your German translations don't come along automatically; re-apply them on the new preview, or ask us and we'll carry them over. This is the same "content edits don't follow the preview" rule as Section 5.4.

10.2 The footer legal links (incl. German Impressum & Widerruf)

The legal links at the very bottom of the footer (Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy, and on the German site Impressum and Vertrag widerrufen) are menus, not hardcoded links:

  • Legal menu - shown on every market (Terms & Conditions, Privacy Policy).
  • Legal menu (German) - shown on the German site only (AGB, Datenschutzrichtlinie, Impressum, Vertrag widerrufen).
  • Manage both under Online Store → Navigation like any other menu. The footer reads whichever menu is selected in its "Legal menu" / "Legal menu (German)" settings (Theme Editor → Footer → Legal).
  • Keep Impressum and Vertrag widerrufen in the German menu; both are legally required for the German store. Treat them as load-bearing; the site also keeps them visible even if they were ever removed.

Confirm you can — tick each one off once you've done it yourself:

11. Users & Permissions (Staff Accounts)

Everyone who logs into your admin is a user with a role. A role is a bundle of permissions, like "can view products", "can edit orders" or "can use the Translate & Adapt app", and you can build a role that fits exactly one job. This is how you let your German translation team in without handing them the keys to the store.

Who can manage users

Only the store owner and users with the Administrator role can add users and edit roles. Your plan (Advanced) allows up to 15 staff accounts (collaborator accounts don't count, see 11.6).

11.1 Adding a new user

  1. Go to Settings → Users (admin.shopify.com/settings/organization-account).
  2. Click Add users. Make sure the Admin and Point of Sale tab is selected.
  3. Enter the person's email address and click Add users.
  4. In Roles, click Assign and pick the role that fits the job. A user can hold more than one role; permissions add up. No role fits yet? Create one first (see 11.3).
  5. Under Two-step authentication, select Required (2FA is already on for your store, see Section 1).
  6. Click Save. They receive an invitation email with a link that expires after 7 days; if it lapses, remove and re-add the user to send a fresh invite.

11.2 The permission model in one minute

Permissions are grouped into areas (Products, Orders, Online store, Content, Files, Apps and sales channels…) with levels per area, usually View, Create and edit, and Delete. Two behaviours to know:

  • Dependencies auto-select. Grant "Products → View" and the Files permission it needs comes along automatically; Shopify highlights what depends on what as you click.
  • Apps are per-app. Under Apps and sales channels you can tick one specific app (e.g. Translate & Adapt) instead of granting "Manage and install apps and channels". That single choice is the difference between "can use the translation app" and "can install and delete any app on the store".

11.3 Recipe: a "German Translation" role (translators, nothing else)

Settings → Users → Roles → Create role, name it e.g. German Translation, then set exactly these permissions:

Permission areaSet toWhy
Apps and sales channels → Translate & Adapt✅ Granted (that app only)Lets them open the translation app. Do not tick "Manage and install apps and channels".
Products → View✅ ViewRequired for Translate & Adapt to show product content (titles, descriptions) for translation. View-only - no prices, no editing.
Online store → Blog posts and pages⚠️ Only if they must translate German pages / blog / policiesThis knob is coarse: it bundles view, create, and delete. If the team is products-only, leave it off.
Online store → Themes⚠️ Only if they must translate theme-editor text (e.g. the announcement bar, footer, see Section 10.1)Also coarse: it includes publish themes. If you don't want a translator publishing a theme, leave it off and do theme text in-house.
Everything else (Orders, Customers, Discounts, Settings, Checkout, Finance…)❌ No accessLeast privilege. They're here to translate, nothing else.
Never grant these to a translation role

Manage and install apps and channels, Edit code, Store settings → Manage settings, Orders, Customers, Finance, and the Administrator role itself. There is no separate "user management" permission; Administrator is the only way to manage users, and it also means full control of everything.

Test with one user before rolling out

Translation access = the app granted plus view access to each resource the team will translate. Create the role, add one test user, sign in as them, open Translate & Adapt and check they can edit the German column for the resources you intended. If a resource type is missing or read-only, grant that area's View permission and retest, then add the rest of the team.

11.4 What a translation-only user can and can't do

CanCan't
Open Translate & Adapt and edit German translations for the resources you grantedEdit product prices, inventory or product content (view-only on Products)
View products in the adminSee orders, customers, discounts, analytics, or settings
Save translations live (they apply to /de-de immediately)Install, remove or manage apps; edit theme code; publish themes
-Add or manage other users

11.5 Removing access (offboarding)

  • Settings → Users → click the user → ⋮ → Deactivate (keeps the account for later reactivation) or Remove (frees the seat).
  • Invitations not accepted within 7 days expire; remove and re-add the user to re-invite.
  • Watch the 15-user plan limit; deactivated or removed users free up a seat.

11.6 External translation agency? Consider collaborator accounts

If your German translators are an external agency, Shopify's cleaner pattern is a collaborator account: the agency's partner account is added as a collaborator with access limited to specific apps (e.g. Translate & Adapt only), and you approve the request. Collaborators don't count against your 15 staff seats. The catch: the agency needs a Shopify Partner account. If they don't have one, plain staff accounts with the 11.3 role are the way to go.

12. Inventory & Stock

Shopify gives you several places that touch stock, and they answer different questions. The short version: quantities live in Inventory, availability lives in Catalogs, and the product page is for quick edits while you happen to be there. Knowing which one to open saves a lot of hunting.

12.1 The Inventory section - your day-to-day home for stock

Products → Inventory lists every SKU with its full stock position, one warehouse at a time. Use the location picker at the top to switch between warehouses. This is the agreed way of working: manage and check quantities here, not product-by-product.

What the columns mean:

ColumnMeaning
AvailableWhat the storefront can sell right now. This is the number you’ll adjust most.
CommittedAllocated to orders that are placed but not yet fulfilled.
UnavailableHeld back on purpose - damaged, reserved, or awaiting inspection.
On handPhysically in the warehouse: available + committed + unavailable.
IncomingOn its way via a purchase order or transfer. Not sellable until received.

To change a quantity, click the number, choose whether you’re correcting the count or recording received stock, and save. You can edit several rows before saving in one go.

12.2 On the product page - quick single edits

Every product’s variants carry their own quantity per location, so you can edit stock from the product screen: open the product, click into a variant, and adjust the quantity for the warehouse in question. That’s handy when you’re already editing the product for another reason - but for anything beyond a one-off, the Inventory section above is faster and shows you the whole picture.

12.3 Catalogs - availability is not stock

A product can be in stock and still invisible in a country, because quantity and availability are two separate levers:

  • Zero stock → the product still appears on the storefront, marked sold out.
  • Excluded from a market’s catalog → the product doesn’t appear in that country at all, however much stock it has.

Markets → Catalogs holds one retail catalog per market. Open a catalog to see (and change) which products are included, or manage it from the product side: the product page’s Publishing card lists the catalogs it belongs to. If you’re ever hunting for a product that’s “missing” from one storefront, check its catalog before anything else.

12.4 Incoming stock - purchase orders & transfers

Two more tabs under Products feed the Incoming column: Purchase orders records stock ordered from a supplier into a warehouse, and Transfers moves stock between your own locations. Receiving against either updates On hand automatically - no manual count adjustment needed.

Low-stock warnings: automated threshold alerts (an email to the right region when an item drops to a set level, before it hits zero) are being set up via Mechanic. Until they’re live, the Inventory section is the place to check stock before it runs out.

Confirm you can - tick each one off once you've done it yourself:

Blind Spots - the things that get missed

These aren't obvious from the core admin, and they're where clients get stuck (or panic) after we leave. We cover them explicitly so you know exactly where your data goes.

Form / enquiry data - where does it go?

The #1 thing to get right

Your Contact page form submits to arbortech@arbortech.com.au. Confirm who monitors this inbox, that it's not hitting spam, and that it's being checked daily. Enquiries that land in an unmonitored inbox are lost enquiries.

  • Contact form (/pages/contact) → emails arbortech@arbortech.com.au. Owner: confirm with Max/Nora.
  • Service / warranty → service@arbortech.com.au (used on the Service/Repair & Warranty page). Owner: confirm.
  • German withdrawal (Widerruf) - the /de-de/pages/widerruf form sends an automated confirmation to the customer via the Mechanic app; there's no admin inbox for it (customer gets the email directly).
  • If an enquiry doesn't arrive, check the spam/junk folder and the address configured in the contact section (Online Store → Themes → Customize → Contact page section → Email field).

Newsletter / marketing sign-ups

Sign-ups live in Mailchimp, not Shopify

Your newsletter capture (footer signup, inline newsletter section, and popup) is wired to Mailchimp. Subscribers also appear as tagged customer records in Shopify (newsletter, arbortechie-club), but the actual audience list and campaigns live in Mailchimp (mailchimp.com). Editing the list, sending campaigns, and managing signup audiences happens there, not in Shopify.

Order & customer notifications

  • Order confirmations and shipping emails to customers are Shopify's built-in transactional templates (Settings → Notifications), sent from the store address steveb@arbortech.com.au (the store contact email, Steve Bell). Confirm that's the address you want customers to see, and that replies aren't going to a stale inbox.
  • Packing slips / warehouse emails are generated by the Mechanic app (daily per-region batches: AU, US, UK, CA, DE). Right now they route to Juicebox test inboxes; at go-live they'll route to your warehouse team's real addresses (Max, Nora, Layla, Gary, David/Brian at Arbortech USA, Treeline USA, Welch Group UK, and the DE channel still to be confirmed). This is configured in Mechanic, not in Shopify admin.
  • Low-stock alerts: there is currently no automated warehouse low-stock alert built. If you want one, that's a request to Juicebox (tracked under the operations epic).

App-driven content

App / ToolWhat it powersWhere you edit it
MechanicPacking-slip emails, Widerruf confirmation, (future) automation tasksMechanic dashboard (usemechanic.com) - Juicebox operates it
MailchimpNewsletter lists, campaigns, signup syncMailchimp dashboard
Stamped.ioProduct reviews (coming soon, currently disabled)Stamped dashboard + enable toggle in Theme Settings
Translate & AdaptGerman translations of products, pages, policiesShopify admin → Settings → Translate & Adapt
Shopify BundlesComposed bundle products (Mini Grinder kits, ALLSAW bundles)Shopify admin → Products → Bundles
Shopify Payments / PayPalPayment processing (PayPal = Germany only)Settings → Payments (call us)
If you can't find it in the page, it's probably an app

Reviews, newsletter audiences, packing slips, translations: anything that isn't a standard Shopify field is almost always edited in an app dashboard, not on the Shopify page. If you hunt in vain, check the table above before assuming it's broken.

No undo / no version history

There is no Ctrl+Z for content

Shopify doesn't keep content history the way a traditional CMS might. Overwrite a description, delete an image, or archive-then-delete a product, and it's gone. Reinforce the habits: draft before publishing, archive instead of delete, and keep your own backups of important copy (e.g. a shared doc) if you'd like a safety net.

URL handles & redirects

Changing a product/page handle breaks the old link (and loses SEO). The fix is a redirect: Online Store → Navigation → URL Redirects → Add redirect, old URL → new URL. If a customer reports a 404, check URL Redirects and the page/product handle before anything else. (Note: Shopify redirects are exact-match, no wildcards; a whole-prefix move needs one redirect per old URL, or a call to us.)

Metafields - the fields that don't look like fields

Edit the right field, or nothing happens

This theme pulls much of its rich content from custom fields (metafields) that don't appear on the standard product/page screen. The big ones:

  • Product story panels - the long image/text story sections on product pages (product_story_sections, with market variants _au, _us, _ca, _de). Editable in the product page under the metafields section, or via the metaobjects (Story panels) in Settings → Custom data.
  • Clever Bits - the small "clever" feature callouts on a product page (same pattern, incl. per-vertical variants).
  • News story layouts (arbortech.story_blocks) - the section-by-section layout of the designed News story articles (text passages, quote banners, galleries, videos). This is a structured data field maintained by Juicebox; on those posts the ordinary Content box is a non-rendering fallback, so ask us for story article changes (see Section 3.3).
  • Short description (arbt.short_description) - the copy shown on collection tiles.
  • Vertical context (arbt.vertical_context) - which audience(s) a product belongs to (woodworking / masonry / landscaping).
  • Pre-order flag (arbt.pre_order) - switches the buy button to pre-order messaging.
  • Related accessories & compatibility (arbortech.related_accessories on tools, arbortech.compatible_with_filter on accessories) - the tool ↔ accessory cross-links, covered step-by-step in Section 2.6.

If a product page shows content that isn't in the description box, it's coming from one of these. If you can't see a field, click View all / the ⋮ menu on the product page → Edit metafields, or check Settings → Custom data for the metaobject forms (Story panels / Clever Bits are edited as forms with rich text + image pickers).

Market option rules (voltage, power versions)

Which variant options customers see per market (e.g. 240V UK, 18V vs 20V) is controlled by market option rules (metaobjects in Settings → Custom data → Market option rule). If a variant you add doesn't show in a particular country, the option value likely isn't in that market's allowed list. Ask us before changing these rules; getting them wrong hides products from a whole market.

Active doesn't always mean visible

A product can say Active, have stock, have a price, and still be completely unreachable on the shop - its own product page returns "page not found", and it appears in no collection, no search result and no filter. Active is only the first of three gates, and all three have to pass:

GateWhere to check itIf it fails
Status is ActiveStatus box, top of the product pageDraft and Archived products are hidden
Published to Online StorePublishing / sales channels box on the productHidden everywhere on the shop
Included in the Australia marketMarkets section of the product's publishing boxHidden on the Australian shop specifically

The third one is the one nobody expects, because nothing on the product looks wrong. We hit exactly this: a sanding-disc product was Active, published, priced, and showed 5,400 units in stock across five sizes - and its page returned "page not found", because it wasn't included in the Australia market.

Often this is on purpose. Around nine products are being deliberately held back from the shop while their SKUs, stock or duplicate records are sorted out. You can spot these by their tags - anything starting arbt- (for example arbt-reconciliation-quarantine, arbt-duplicate-product) or tagged scope-review is on hold by design. Please don't publish those without checking with us; the tag is there to stop a half-finished product reaching customers.

So if a product seems to be missing from the shop: check the three gates above before you touch anything else, and look at its tags to see whether it's being held back on purpose. If it has no arbt- or scope-review tag and still isn't visible, that's worth reporting to us.

Draft vs live confusion

Thing"Not yet live" stateHow to tell
ProductDraft / ArchivedStatus label on the product
Page / Blog postDraft or ScheduledStatus label; scheduled shows a date
Theme changeSaved on unpublished themeTheme list shows which theme is live; "Customize" opens whichever theme you selected

When in doubt, open the storefront in a private window and look. If it's not there, it's draft/scheduled/archived/on the wrong theme.

Legal & policy pages

Privacy Policy, Terms & Conditions, Refund/Returns, Shipping, Cookies Policy, and the German legal pages (e.g. Widerruf, Impressum) are your responsibility to keep current. They're standard pages under Online Store → Pages, and some (privacy, refund policy, T&Cs) are Shopify policies under Settings → Policies. Confirm who owns keeping them updated.

Mobile

Preview on mobile before publishing

Most of your traffic is mobile. A banner that looks great on desktop can break on a phone. In the Theme Editor use the device toggle (desktop ↔ mobile) to check every change; in page/blog editors use Preview on a phone too. Also check the mega-menus and variant pickers on mobile; they collapse into different layouts.

Guardrails - what NOT to touch

Call these out clearly so nothing breaks:

AreaWhy
Theme code / Edit code (Online Store → Themes → ⋮ → Edit code)Any Liquid/CSS/JS change can break the whole site. All code changes go through Juicebox's GitHub workflow.
Checkout, payment, shipping and tax settings (Settings → Payments / Shipping / Taxes, Checkout)Configures how you get paid and what customers pay. Errors here are expensive. Call us.
App installs / uninstalls and integrationsUninstalling an app can remove its data and break theme features (e.g. Mailchimp, Mechanic). Ask first.
Domain and DNS settingsWrong DNS takes the whole site down. Call us.
Deleting products, collections, or pagesNo undo, no history. Archive instead.
Publishing a themeWe manage the live/preview theme workflow. You edit content on the published preview; you never hit Publish.
Adding staff accounts with full permissions (Settings → Users)Every full-access user is a risk surface. Use roles (Section 11): give people the least access that does their job, e.g. the German translation team gets Translate & Adapt + Products view, nothing else.
